study_subtitle: Concept Testing Report · Personal Finance MVP
single_sentence_takeaway: Pair real-time fraud alerts with shared partner tagging to cover the portfolio — but firm up fraud with a second round before committing the roadmap.
research_question: Which concepts most credibly serve customer needs for tracking recurring expenses, catching fraud, and sharing financial state with a partner?
method_description: Concept testing — past-use stories + per-need usefulness ratings
usage_guidance: Use for the MVP-scope conversation with product, design, and engineering leads. Each recommendation maps to a roadmap decision; treat sparse-coverage flags as a sequencing risk, not an indictment.

needs.statement: Track recurring expenses across all my accounts
needs.label: Track recurring expenses

needs.statement: Catch fraudulent or anomalous charges quickly
needs.label: Catch fraud quickly

needs.statement: Share day-to-day financial state with my partner
needs.label: Share with partner

insights.insight: No single concept covers the full need set — the portfolio only works as a pair.

evidence.metric: 0 of 3 concepts address ≥2 of 3 needs at high confidence

evidence.snippet: If you stick with the tagging it's the cleanest view possible.

insights.so_what: Building any one of these alone leaves at least two of three needs underserved — the MVP framing has to be a set, not a single winner.
insights.recommendation: Plan the roadmap as a concept pair (most likely Smart spend alerts + Manual transaction tagger) and design the joint experience, not just the individual concepts.

insights.insight: Smart spend alerts has the strongest fraud signal — but the evidence is sparse.

evidence.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.
evidence.source_ref: Smart spend alerts × Catch fraud quickly
Smart spend alerts × Catch fraud quickly

evidence.metric: n=3 of 5 (study ran out of time)

insights.so_what: Smart spend alerts is the only concept that addresses fraud, and the same anomaly mechanism is a positive surprise on recurring-expense tracking — but the n is too thin to commit on alone.
insights.recommendation: Run a focused second round to bring Smart spend alerts to n=5 before locking it into the MVP.

insights.insight: Manual transaction tagger owns partner sharing — but at a real adoption cost.

evidence.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
evidence.source_ref: Manual transaction tagger × Share with partner

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money.
evidence.source_ref: Manual transaction tagger × Catch fraud quickly

insights.so_what: Manual transaction tagger is the only concept that resolves shared categorization disputes — but tagging-as-mechanism is adoption-fragile and, for at least one participant, anxiety-inducing.
insights.recommendation: Iterate Manual transaction tagger toward auto-suggested defaults with manual override, then re-test with anxiety-prone users specifically.

insights.insight: Automation and low-effort concepts were preferred wherever they appeared.

evidence.snippet: Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.
If it knows your normal spending it knows your subscriptions, so why not.

evidence.metric: Automation cited as the up-driver on Weekly auto-digest (4 of 5) and on Smart spend alerts (3 of 3)

insights.so_what: Across concepts, the no-effort affordance is what participants rated up — and it shows up regardless of the surface (email digest, push alert). This is the dominant axis underneath the matrix.
insights.recommendation: Make auto-behavior the default in every concept; reserve manual control for override, not for setup.

insights.insight: Manual effort is claimed in theory and rejected in practice.

evidence.snippet: Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.
evidence.source_ref: Manual transaction tagger × Track recurring expenses

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money.
evidence.source_ref: Manual transaction tagger × Catch fraud quickly

evidence.metric: 4 of 5 participants cited tagging burden as a down-driver on Manual transaction tagger

insights.so_what: Where the concept asked for input (Manual transaction tagger), most participants said they'd rate it generously in theory but wouldn't follow through. The aspirational-vs-actual gap is structural.
insights.recommendation: Don't ship any concept whose value is gated on per-transaction manual work — fold the value into an auto-suggest layer with one-tap override.

insights.insight: Weekly auto-digest's cadence is structurally wrong for fraud.

evidence.snippet: A weekly email is way too late. Fraud needs to be in seconds, not days.
If I see fraud on Monday, this email doesn't help me until Friday.

insights.so_what: Weekly auto-digest owns its target need (tracking recurring expenses) at the lowest effort cost in the portfolio — but the weekly cadence makes it fundamentally wrong for the fraud framing it was given.
insights.recommendation: Drop Weekly auto-digest's fraud framing in copy and subject lines; pair it with Smart spend alerts (which absorbs the fraud signal in real time) in the MVP brief.

insights.insight: Roommate-style sharing is an unmet need the portfolio doesn't see.

evidence.snippet: Honestly the thing I really need is a way to split rent and groceries with my roommates without a shared spreadsheet.
I want something for that — a way to set up shared recurring obligations with people who aren't my partner.

evidence.metric: 2 of 5 surfaced it unprompted; missed by Weekly auto-digest, Manual transaction tagger, and Smart spend alerts

insights.so_what: The sharing need as scoped assumes a romantic-partnership context; 40% of participants surfaced a non-romantic-cohabitant variant. The portfolio doesn't address it, and demographic trends suggest the gap is widening.
insights.recommendation: Scope a discovery study on roommate / non-romantic shared finance before the next concept round.

insights.insight: Smart spend alerts + Manual transaction tagger is the smallest concept set that covers the full plan.

evidence.metric: Smart spend alerts covers tracking + fraud; Manual transaction tagger covers sharing — together they cover all three plan needs

insights.so_what: Building Weekly auto-digest alone leaves fraud and sharing unsolved. Building Smart spend alerts alone leaves sharing unsolved. Only this pair has full plan coverage.
insights.recommendation: Frame the next leadership review as MVP = Smart spend alerts + Manual transaction tagger, with Weekly auto-digest as a candidate for a later release.

insights.insight: Manual transaction tagger introduced money anxiety for one participant — small signal, big risk.

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money — I'd be anxious about getting it wrong, missing one, mis-tagging it.
evidence.source_ref: Manual transaction tagger × Catch fraud quickly

insights.so_what: Tagging-as-mechanism, intended to give control, instead introduced money anxiety for an anxiety-prone participant. One strong signal of a concept making the user's relationship to the need worse is enough to surface for follow-up, regardless of majority verdict.
insights.recommendation: Recruit anxiety-prone participants explicitly for the Manual transaction tagger re-test; treat the auto-suggest iteration as a hypothesis that the anxiety dissolves once the per-transaction work goes away.

concepts.name: Weekly auto-digest
concepts.description: A weekly email that automatically categorizes the past week's spending and shows changes from the prior week. No interaction required.

target_needs.hypothesis: Auto-categorization makes recurring spend visible without manual work
Weekly review surfaces anomalies the user might otherwise miss

concepts.top_finding: Low-effort pulse check on recurring spend, appreciated — but the wrong cadence for fraud.

recommendation.statement: Keep Weekly auto-digest as the low-effort recurring-expense surface; drop the fraud framing entirely and pair it with Smart spend alerts for real-time signal.

recommended_refinements: Aggregate joint and personal accounts in the same digest so household recurring spend is in one place.
Surface week-over-week deltas more prominently than absolute totals — the change is the story.
Drop the 'fraud catch' framing from the email subject line and body copy.
Test Sunday-morning vs Monday-morning send times for engagement.

concepts.name: Manual transaction tagger
concepts.description: Users tag every transaction with a custom category as it comes in. Tags are sharable with a partner who sees the same tagged feed.

target_needs.hypothesis: Manual control yields cleaner, user-defined categories
Shared tags align partners on what counts as what

concepts.top_finding: Owns partner sharing — at a real adoption cost.

recommendation.statement: Iterate toward auto-suggested category defaults with manual override; re-test with anxiety-prone recruits before any MVP commit.

recommended_refinements: Prototype auto-suggested tag defaults with one-tap override instead of tag-from-scratch.
Replace 'tag every transaction' framing with 'review weekly batches' to lower the perceived effort floor.
Seed each new account with a partner-shared category dictionary so day-one isn't blank.
Recruit anxiety-prone users explicitly for the next round; the P03 signal needs to be probed, not dismissed.

concepts.name: Smart spend alerts
concepts.description: Real-time push notifications when an algorithm detects a transaction that looks unusual relative to your normal spend. User can dismiss, confirm-fraud, or mark-as-expected.

target_needs.hypothesis: Real-time anomaly detection catches fraud at the moment it happens

concepts.top_finding: Best single bet on fraud — evidence-sparse, but uniformly positive.

recommendation.statement: Strongest single concept in the portfolio — run a focused second round to n=5 before locking it into the MVP.

recommended_refinements: Add 'mark as expected' as a quick action on the alert itself to reduce alert fatigue for recurring-but-legit charges.
Probe explicitly in screening for the automation-distrust pattern P02 surfaced.
Test contextual depth — how much per-alert context is too much vs too little.
Run a second round to n=5 on the existing concept first; no design change before evidence is firm.
concepts.dist_note: Note: Sparse coverage (study ran out of time). All Smart spend alerts verdicts carry medium-or-lower confidence as a result.

evidence.snippet: I would have loved this last month — I would've seen the Spotify thing immediately.
Auto-categorization is exactly what I want. I'm never going to do it myself.

findings.notes: Strong consensus that auto-categorization is the key driver. P05 halo applied (see Methodology · Study observations) — does not undermine the verdict but does not strengthen it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Majority `partially` (3/5) with consistent explanations citing weekly cadence. P05 halo applied; P02's `not_at_all` reinforces the cadence concern. Held at `partial`.

evidence.snippet: It might catch some stuff but if I see fraud on Monday, this email doesn't help me until Friday.
A weekly email is way too late. Fraud needs to be in seconds, not days.

findings.notes: Cadence is the bottleneck. The concept was designed to surface anomalies but the weekly delivery rhythm fundamentally limits effectiveness. Consider a real-time fallback for high-value anomalies.

findings.reconciliation_note: P05 halo applied. 4/5 explicit `not_at_all` with consistent explanations confirms the verdict.

evidence.snippet: This is just for me. My partner would never see it.
Email is one-way. There's no shared aspect to it.

findings.notes: Concept was not targeted at sharing and unanimously confirmed not to address it.

findings.reconciliation_note: Designed-vs-actual gap on adoption likelihood: ratings (2 completely, 3 partially) reflect that participants understand tagging would give the cleanest view, but most explicitly state they wouldn't actually do the tagging. P03's explanation cell was empty — flagged but does not change the verdict.

evidence.snippet: If I'm tagging things anyway I'd put 'subscription' on the recurring ones — clearer than auto-categorization.
Theoretically the cleanest. In practice I won't do it.

findings.notes: The disconnect between theoretical and practical addressing is the dominant signal. Manual transaction tagger was designed for tracking recurring expenses but the manual-effort cost makes adoption fragile.

findings.reconciliation_note: Raw majority was `not_at_all` (4/5), which would normally yield `doesn't address`. P03's explanation explicitly describes the concept as anxiety-inducing — even one strong instance of the concept making the user's relationship to the need worse triggers `creates new problem` per the verdict rules. Confidence is low because the signal is from one participant; surfaced because creates-new-problem is reportable at any confidence.

evidence.snippet: Tagging every transaction would stress me out, especially around money — I'd be anxious about getting it wrong, missing one, mis-tagging it.

findings.notes: Single strong signal — surfaced for further investigation. The risk is that tagging-as-mechanism, intended to give control, instead introduces money anxiety. Test in a follow-up study with anxiety-prone users specifically.

evidence.snippet: Same tags, same view, finally a way to align on what counts as 'eating out'.
If my roommate could see the same tags this would solve the entire shared-grocery argument.
We'd both see the same tagged feed — that's the whole solution.

findings.notes: Manual transaction tagger delivers on its target. The shared-tags mechanism resolves an explicit pain (categorization disputes) that participants had concrete past-use stories about. Note that P02's quote drifts toward roommates — see emergent-need card on the Weekly auto-digest tab.

findings.reconciliation_note: n=3 (sparse) but 2 completely + 1 partially with consistent reasoning that 'an algorithm that knows your normal spend also knows your recurring stuff.' Not targeted, but the addresses verdict holds.

evidence.snippet: If you're catching every weird charge, you're also catching the recurring stuff that drifts.
If it knows your normal spending it knows your subscriptions, so why not.

findings.notes: Good surprise — Smart spend alerts was designed only for fraud, but the same anomaly-detection mechanism surfaces recurring-charge changes as a side effect.

findings.reconciliation_note: All 3 raters said `completely` with consistent positive reasoning around real-time + contextual content. Confidence is medium rather than high due to small n. P02's contradictory explanation is logged at study level (see Methodology · Study observations).

evidence.snippet: Real-time alerts with context — that's exactly what fraud detection should feel like.
Real-time and contextual — that's exactly the right shape.

findings.notes: Smart spend alerts delivers on its single targeted need. The contextual alert content (showing what the charge is) was consistently called out as the differentiator from generic bank alerts.

findings.reconciliation_note: Only P01 rated this cell (1× not_at_all). Below the 2-participant threshold for actionable evidence.

evidence.snippet: It's a notification on my phone. My partner doesn't see my phone.

findings.notes: Direction is negative but the cell is structurally under-evidenced. Not actionable.

emergent_needs.label: Splitting recurring shared expenses with roommates
emergent_needs.confidence_note: Surfaced unprompted in 2/5 past-use stories (P02, P04); both returned to it spontaneously

evidence.snippet: Honestly the thing I really need is a way to split rent and groceries with my roommates without a shared spreadsheet.
I want something for that — a way to set up shared recurring obligations with people who aren't my partner.

emergent_needs.commentary: The "share with partner" need as scoped assumes a romantic-partnership context. 40% of participants surfaced a roommate / non-romantic-cohabitant need without prompting. The portfolio doesn't address it — and given the demographic shift toward later partnership, this gap may be larger than this study can size. Worth scoping a discovery study.

halo_participants.rationale: P05 rated completely across nearly every cell with vague, generic explanations ("sounds good", "this would help"). This is consistent with halo / acquiescence rather than considered judgment. Their ratings were down-weighted in every per-cell reconciliation. Treat P05's data as directional only — not as one of five equal data points.

sparse_coverage.rationale: Smart spend alerts was rated by only 3 of 5 participants because the study ran out of time. This is why every Smart spend alerts verdict carries medium-or-lower confidence even when the signal is uniformly positive. A follow-up round bringing this concept to n=5 is the cheapest way to firm up the strongest single concept in the portfolio.

contradictions.rationale: P02 rated Smart spend alerts completely on fraud while saying "I don't really trust automated alerts" in the same breath. Logged as a known contradiction worth probing, not as an undermining signal — the rating itself was for the concept's shape, the comment was about a category-level skepticism.
contradictions.snippet: I don't really trust automated alerts. I always second-guess them.

study_setup.format: 60-minute moderated 1:1 sessions. Each session opened with a past-use story for each need, followed by stimulus-based concept presentation, followed by per-need ratings with explanations.
study_setup.sample: 5 participants, recruited for active personal-finance app use and at least one shared-spending context (partner or roommate). Mix of household structures.
study_setup.needs_tested: 3 functional outcomes from the team's job-map work.
